title: About
description: My work has moved from understanding how people move, to asking how future physiotherapists learn to think, decide, and care.
content: My work has moved from understanding how people move, to asking how future physiotherapists learn to think, decide, and care. Why physiotherapy Physiotherapy first attracted me because it joins scientific understanding with practical human judgement. Movement can be measured, but good care still depends on listening, reasoning, adapting, and seeing the person rather than only the condition. Why education Teaching made the hidden work of clinical reasoning impossible to ignore. Students did not only need more information; they needed opportunities to explain decisions, test assumptions, make mistakes safely, and connect theory with the person in front of them. Why virtual reality VR offered a way to make difficult, spatial, or rarely encountered experiences more available. My interest is not in immersion for its own sake. It is in whether a designed experience helps students notice, practise, and understand something that other methods cannot show as clearly. Why artificial intelligence AI raises a different challenge. It can expand feedback and generate possibilities, but it can also hide weak reasoning behind fluent answers. I am interested in designs that make students think before consulting AI, question what it produces, and remain accountable for the final judgement. How can we design learning experiences that make clinical reasoning visible, preserve meaningful human judgement, and use technology only where it adds genuine educational value? Start with the learner Define the competence, misconception, or barrier before choosing a tool. Make thinking visible Ask students to explain, compare, defend, and revise their decisions. Design for transfer Connect classroom activity to the uncertainty and responsibility of professional practice. Evaluate honestly Treat friction, failure, and unintended consequences as evidence for the next design. title: Research
description: These projects bring together physiotherapy, AI, VR, simulation, and educational design around one goal: improving how students develop and demonstrate clinical reasoning.
content: I want to be known for designing evidence-informed ways to integrate AI and VR into physiotherapy education without allowing technology to replace the thinking students must learn to do. Virtual Reality Acupuncture Turning a spatial and safety-sensitive skill into a structured cycle of preparation, practice, and assessment. Students need repeated opportunities to connect anatomy, point location, safety, and procedural reasoning, but access to guided practice is limited by time, place, and supervision. A curriculum-aligned VR application with training, practice, and assessment modes, supported by preparation and debriefing rather than treated as a stand-alone simulation. Spatial orientation, anatomical relationships, procedural sequence, safety decisions, and explanation of technique. Educational designer and lecturer supporting development and curriculum integration. Current project: development and curriculum integration. Which parts of the learning experience are improved by immersion, and which still require direct teaching and physical practice? AI Literacy for Health Professionals Helping learners verify, disclose, question, and remain accountable for AI-supported work. Using a chatbot is not the same as understanding hallucination, bias, privacy, verification, or professional accountability. A developing sequence of curriculum prompts, reflective writing, and a short interactive knowledge check that makes responsible-use decisions concrete. Source verification, privacy judgement, bias awareness, disclosure, appropriate task selection, and responsibility for final decisions. Lecturer and educational designer developing practical AI-literacy activities. Active teaching resource and curriculum-development theme. How should practical AI literacy be assessed without reducing it to tool familiarity or policy recall? Clinical Reasoning Chatbot Designing AI to ask better questions before it offers answers. AI can produce plausible clinical answers before students have identified red flags, compared hypotheses, or justified a plan. A pilot chatbot that prioritises safety screening, staged questioning, explanation, and reflection before suggestions are revealed. Red-flag recognition, hypothesis generation, evidence use, prioritisation, explanation, and critical review of AI output. Researcher and educational designer leading the pilot concept and learning design. Pilot study in development; no claims of effectiveness are made yet. Can structured AI dialogue improve the visibility and quality of student reasoning without creating over-reliance? Teaching Human Physiology with VR Using immersion to connect structure, function, movement, and clinical meaning. Dynamic physiological relationships can remain abstract when students encounter them only as diagrams, slides, or isolated facts. Short immersive encounters embedded within a wider lesson: preparation, guided observation, case application, peer explanation, and debriefing. Three-dimensional relationships, structure-function connections, observation, explanation, and transfer to clinical cases. Lecturer designing and refining the surrounding learning sequence. Teaching approach under iterative development. What is the smallest useful dose of immersion, and how should the surrounding lesson be designed to make it count? Simulation in Health Professional Education Exploring how different simulation roles may direct attention towards different aspects of learning. Simulation learning is often discussed mainly in relation to the student performing as the clinician, while less is known about what students may learn as peer patients, observers, or peer debriefers. A structured role-rotation model involving Learner, Peer Patient, Observer, and Peer Debriefer roles, supported by role preparation, focused observation, guided reflection, and educator oversight for clinical accuracy and psychological safety. Early student accounts suggest different emphases across roles: clinical integration, patient-centred awareness, analytical distance, and feedback dialogue. These are perceived learning possibilities rather than confirmed effects. Researcher and lecturer contributing to the role-rotation design and ongoing analysis. Ongoing analysis and manuscript development; effects on clinical competence and readiness have not been established. Do role-specific learning experiences transfer to later simulation or clinical practice, and how can this be measured beyond self-report? It argues that implementation depends on curriculum alignment, scaffolding, and institutional support rather than hardware alone. title: Should We Assess Students With AI — or Without It?
description: A two-lane approach reframes AI assessment around purpose: support learning with contemporary tools, then assure independent clinical capability where it matters.
content: Should We Assess Students With AI — or Without It? A two-lane approach reframes AI assessment around purpose: support learning with contemporary tools, then assure independent clinical capability where it matters. One of the questions I keep returning to in health professions education is: If students are going to use AI in their future practice, should we allow them to use it during assessment? The University of Sydney's approach caught my attention because, rather than treating AI as simply allowed or prohibited , it separates assessment into two different lanes. Two lanes with different purposes In the open lane , students can make appropriate use of contemporary tools, including generative AI. These assessments recognise that knowing how to work critically and responsibly with AI is increasingly becoming part of professional practice. The secure lane , however, serves a different purpose. Here, students demonstrate what they can do independently under supervised conditions. This can include written examinations, oral assessments, practical examinations, OSCE-type activities and observed clinical performance. I find this distinction particularly relevant to physiotherapy education. Perhaps we do not need every assessment to prove that a student can work without AI. But somewhere in the programme, we still need to be confident that the student standing in front of a patient can reason, communicate, examine and make decisions independently . AI may have an important role before assurance At the same time, there is growing evidence that AI may have an important role before that point. A 2026 randomised study involving 80 medical students compared conventional standardised-patient training with an approach combining standardised patients and AI virtual standardised patients. Students receiving the blended training demonstrated greater improvements in clinical reasoning, core competencies and OSCE performance in this study. What I find most interesting is that the study does not necessarily make the case for replacing human simulation with AI. It makes a case for blending them . A possible educational pathway AI virtual patients could provide students with repeated, accessible opportunities to practise clinical reasoning, make mistakes, explore alternative decisions and receive feedback. Human simulation and clinical encounters can then introduce the communication, unpredictability, emotional complexity and interpersonal judgement that are much harder to replicate. Finally, secure assessment can answer the most important question: Can the student actually do this when the AI is no longer there? Learn with AI → practise with AI → practise with people → demonstrate independently → enter clinical practice. Start with what the assessment must prove For me, this changes the AI assessment conversation. Rather than asking whether AI should be permitted or banned, perhaps we should first ask what each assessment is supposed to prove . If the purpose is learning, experimentation, feedback and development, AI may have considerable value. If the purpose is to assure ourselves that a future healthcare professional can perform safely and independently, then there must still be moments when the student, not the AI, has to demonstrate that capability. The challenge now is deciding where those moments should sit within the curriculum. Perhaps that is where programme-level assessment design becomes much more important than trying to redesign every individual assignment in response to AI. Related reading University of Sydney.
